newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Berlin's top hotel emerges from the ashes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Berlin's top hotel emerges from the ashes.

text.p: Albert Einstein looks down from the first floor landing of the Hotel Adlon while guests sip tea and coffee around a fountain in the lobby below.
The scene could be from the Berlin of the interwar years, when the famous physicist was one of many illustrious guests at the city's top hotel, in the shadow of the Brandenburg Gate.
But the setting is the present day. Fifty-two years after it was burnt down by Russian soldiers, the Hotel Adlon is back.

The management may not have succeeded in resurrecting Einstein -- the man on the balcony is a lookalike laid on for a reception to recall the hotel's famous past -- but they have gone to great lengths to recreate the style of the old Adlon.

They haven't quite finished. While guests pad across the thick carpets to reception, building workers outside are clambering up scaffolding and hammering stone on the terraces to get the place ready for next month's grand opening ceremony.
Guests can stay at a reduced rate while the workermen put the finishing touches to the hotel before German President Roman Herzog performs the inauguration on August 23.
After that, prices will start at 420 marks ($238) a night for a single room, rising to 1,500 marks for a suite with a view of the Brandenburg Gate and the Pariser Platz square.

At those rates, it is unlikely that most tourists who flock to one of Berlin's most historic areas will ever make it beyond the marble foyer. "It's going to be people who have more money," hotel spokeswoman Sabine Kalkmann acknowledged.
But that, too, is in keeping with the traditions of the old Adlon, which was always a home for the rich and famous visitor to Berlin rather than for the average traveller.
FROM GARBO TO GOEBBELS
Film stars such as Charlie Chaplin, Douglas Fairbanks and Greta Garbo entered their names in the guest book alongside Thomas Mann, Theodore Roosevelt and T.E.Lawrence (of Arabia).
The original hotel, named after owner Lorenz Adlon, opened its doors in 1907. Its first guest was Kaiser Wilhelm II, who became one of its most frequent patrons.
The Adlon set high standards, with such luxuries as hot and cold running water in every room and its own electricty sub station to make sure the lights never went out.
The hotel survived World War Two, becoming an oasis from Allied bombing raids for foreign correspondents, diplomats and even Nazi officials.
But the building fared less well in peacetime. Soon after the end of the war, Russian soldiers raided the Adlon's fabled wine cellar and set the hotel on fire.
"Nobody knows if they did it on purpose but it went up in flames," Kalkmann said.
The tale is also typical of so many associated with the hotel. They may be apocryphal or they may be only part of the truth but they have all contributed to the Adlon legend.
Did Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels really keep his two mistresses in adjacent rooms? Did he buy a bed from the Adlon for his own home because he slept so well there?
Was the voice of legendary Italian tenor Enrico Caruso revived by the pasta and tomato sauce of an Adlon chef?
And did Adlon's son, Louis, recommend the then-unknown Marlene Dietrich to a film director, who cast her in the role of Lola in The Blue Angel which was to make her world famous?

For the new Adlon's owners, the Cologne-based Fundus property company, and its mangers, Kempinski Hotels group, the accuracy of the stories is not what counts. They have all contributed to a brand image second to none in Berlin.
OLD STYLE FOR A NEW AGE

During the Cold War, the site of the Adlon lay derelict on wasteland on the eastern side of the Berlin Wall, at the end of the Unter Den Linden boulevard. "In East Germany, nobody wanted a really luxurious hotel," Kalkmann said.
The fall of the wall in November 1989 made the idea of a new Adlon on the old site a reality. It took around two and a half years to build at a cost of 435 million marks.
The new building looks similar to the original, complete with prematurely-aged sloping green copper roof. But an extra floor has been added and the interior has been redesigned.
"It's completely new but with elements of the old hotel," is Kalkmann's description.
The new hotel offers its guests their own cellular phone so they can be contacted wherever they are in the building. An electronic key card system opens the doors to its 337 rooms.
Its sumptuous facilities include a large ballroom which already has bookings for several state visits. Hidden behind the scenes are built-in television uplinks for live broadcasts.
Managers hope the Adlon's proximity to the new government quarter will make it the natural choice for visiting dignitaries when the parliament and ministries move from Bonn in 1999.
The U.S., French and British embassies are being built on Pariser Platz so diplomats are also set to return to the Adlon. And the hotel has not forgotten its more humble former regulars.
"We've already been in contact with the foreign press association in Berlin about them holding a weekly event here," Kalkmann said. "We wanted to pick up this tradition again."
($ = 1.763 German Marks)
